hints: Calculate the volume of the spherical drop from its radius before relating volume to mass and density.
Use m = ρV, keeping the radius in metres and the density in kg m⁻³.
walkthrough: The volume of a sphere is V = (4/3)πr³.
To two significant figures, the mass is 6.8 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses mass as density multiplied by volume.
Uses the spherical volume from the 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ m radius and density 940 kg m⁻³ to obtain 6.8 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg.

hints: Compare the proposed charge magnitude with the elementary charge carried by one electron.
walkthrough: Charge is quantised: an object's charge magnitude must be an integer multiple of the elementary charge e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
The proposed value, 8.0 × 10⁻²⁰ C, is smaller than one elementary charge and is not an integer multiple of e.
It is therefore impossible for the oil drop to have this charge magnitude.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the minimum non-zero charge magnitude is one elementary charge, 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

hints: Use the uniform-field relationship between potential difference, field strength and plate separation.
Convert 8.0 mm to metres before multiplying by 2.1 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹.
walkthrough: For a uniform electric field between parallel plates, V = Ed.
Convert the separation: d = 8.0 mm = 8.0 × 10⁻³ m.
The potential difference is 1.7 × 10³ V.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses V = Ed for the uniform electric field.
Converts 8.0 mm to 8.0 × 10⁻³ m and obtains 1.7 × 10³ V.

hints: Use the fact that the downward velocity is constant to decide whether the oil drop accelerates.
Then relate zero acceleration to the resultant force.
walkthrough: The oil drop moves with constant velocity, so its acceleration is zero.
Using F = ma, zero acceleration means that the resultant force on the drop is zero.
A zero resultant force means that the drop is in dynamic equilibrium.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that the constant velocity gives zero resultant force, so the drop is in equilibrium.

hints: The constant velocity established in part (ii) means that the upward electric force balances the downward weight.
Equate mg and |q|E, then use the field direction to determine the sign of the charge.
walkthrough: The constant downward velocity means the resultant force is zero, so the upward electric force balances the weight: |q|E = mg.
Rearrange to obtain |q| = mg / E.
The electric field is downward in the diagram, whereas the electric force must be upward to balance the weight; the charge is therefore negative.
The charge on the oil drop is −3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses equilibrium to equate the weight and electric-force magnitudes, for example mg = |q|E.
Uses m = 6.8 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg, g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹ and E = 2.1 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ to obtain a charge magnitude of 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
States that the oil drop has negative charge.

hints: The plate separation is unchanged, so a smaller potential difference means a weaker uniform electric field.
Compare the smaller electric force with the unchanged weight of the oil drop.
walkthrough: For the same plate separation, decreasing the potential difference decreases the electric field strength.
The charge on the oil drop is unchanged, so the upward electric force |q|E decreases.
Its weight is unchanged and is now greater than the upward electric force, giving a downward resultant force.
The resultant downward force causes the oil drop to accelerate downwards.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that reducing the potential difference decreases the electric force on the oil drop.
States that the weight is then greater than the electric force, or that the resultant force is downward.

knowledge_refs.formula_empty_justification: Field-line spacing is a qualitative representation of electric-field strength; no registered major formula directly represents this diagram convention.

hints: The field remains uniform, so its lines remain straight and parallel; decide how their spacing represents a weaker field.
walkthrough: Reducing the potential difference with the plate separation unchanged makes the uniform electric field weaker.
A weaker field is represented by a lower density of field lines.
The field lines therefore remain straight and parallel but become more widely spaced.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the separation between the field lines increases, or that the lines become more widely spaced.

knowledge_refs.formula_empty_justification: This is a force-name identification from the stated air interaction; no calculation or major reusable formula is required.

hints: Identify the force from the air that can act on an object whether or not it is moving.
walkthrough: Air is a fluid, so it exerts an upward buoyant force on an immersed oil drop even when the drop is stationary.
This force is called upthrust.

ai_rubric.observable: States that force X is upthrust.

knowledge_refs.formula_empty_justification: This is a force-name identification from the stated need for motion through air; no calculation or major reusable formula is required.

hints: Identify the force caused by moving through air that is absent when the oil drop is stationary.
walkthrough: A force that requires the oil drop to move through air is caused by the air resisting that motion.
This force is air resistance, also called drag or viscous force.

ai_rubric.observable: States air resistance, drag or viscous force for force Y.
